source.title: Understanding Weight Similarity of Neural Networks via Chain Normalization Rule and Hypothesis-Training-Testing
source.authors: Guang-Cong Wang; Guang-Cong Wang; Wenqi Liang; Jian-Huang Lai

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies similarity between trained network weights, not similarity between input representations or shared features/subspaces. It cites work on convergent learning but does not test the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported experiments measure how well a classifier or retrieval system can identify network-weight sets after chain normalization. These results bear on weight-space similarity, a related but different construct, so rows are marked versions ["none"] and summarized under fits_no_version. The paper does not report input-distance alignment, cross-modal alignment, shared features, or representation interchangeability.
record.test_reason: The study measures permutation-normalized weight-space identifiability: whether a trained classifier can tell which learning task produced a set of weights across repeated SGD runs. It does not compare input representations, activations, features or subspaces across seeds or models. Its result is weaker than cross-seed convergence: same-task weights only need to be closer to each other than to other tasks' weights. This is a related but different construct, so no version is tested. Li et al. (Convergent Learning, an original source) is only cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SGD solutions of an identical network are similar in a learned weight metric space across MLP, CNN and RNN. Two refinements: in Sec 4.4 the hypothesis still holds for all three variants (Res5, Leaky, Depth); the residual-network impact appears only in cross-network classification.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a weight-space normalization and classification/retrieval procedure; it does not apply the original studies' input-representation similarity methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported weight-similarity results vary with normalization: chain-normalized weights generally yield high classification and retrieval accuracy, whereas unnormalized layer weights perform substantially worse. Cross-network classification is also qualitatively affected by changing PlainNet-5 to Res5, but less by the Leaky and Depth variants.

fits_no_version.finding: Chain-normalized weights (W1…Wl Wl^T…W1^T) from 100 repeated SGD runs per task are classified by task with about 96–100% accuracy and retrieved for unseen tasks at about 95–99% rank-1, across MLP, CNN, GRU and ResNet-MLP-12.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Permutation-invariant weight statistics of same-architecture networks trained from different seeds are task-specific and consistent across runs.

fits_no_version.finding: Without permutation normalization, layer weights beyond the first are nearly unidentifiable (about 2–15%); the first layer is moderately identifiable (62.9% and 85.3% for MLP).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Raw weights differ across seeds mainly through neuron permutation symmetry.

fits_no_version.finding: A weight classifier trained on PlainNet-5 transfers to Leaky and Depth variants, but accuracy drops for Res5. Cross-network retrieval is described as robust to all three variants.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-space similarity across architectural variants depends on the change (residual connections vs activation or depth).

record.problems: The evidence is specific to the paper's learned weight classifier and its chain-normalized weight metric; it does not measure input representations. Numeric outcomes for some cross-network comparisons are shown only in figures, and the text provides qualitative summaries rather than separate numbers. The reported experiments do not provide uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: The paper gives additional per-variant numerical results in Figure 4 for local weight classification and retrieval on Res5, Leaky, and Depth, and Figure 5 contains cross-network plots. Those figure values were not transcribed where the supplied text did not support reliable assignment of every plotted number to a condition; the qualitative cross-network outcomes are recorded in r36-r37.

untested.parts: No scaling of size or capability; no comparison of representations across architectures, objectives or data.
Compares normalized weights via task-classification accuracy, not shared features or subspaces of activations across seeds; no unit-level matching analysis.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test between models.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features or circuits.
Normalization dependence concerns weight-space identifiability, not representational similarity metrics.
No measure of the degree or plateau of representational alignment, or of its causes.

record.verdict_notes: T6/cites_only kept. The weight Gram-type normalization is loosely related to V3's shared subspaces, but the test measures task-discriminability of weights, not cross-seed representational similarity. No row bears on any version. Rows left out (Figure 4 per-variant values) also bear on no version. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No scaling of model size or capability, and no comparison of input representations across independently trained models.
No vision-language model comparison or paired image-caption representation alignment.
The study compares weights of same-task training runs, not learned input features or shared representation subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired representation interchangeability test.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Similarity settings are varied for weight-space classification and retrieval, not for input-representation convergence.
No test of representation alignment plateauing or of shared data/objectives as its cause.
